findings.reason: a node implementing §8 from this sentence builds the cycle graph without the section → implementing-request edge and ships a silent deadlock instead of a queue-time refusal, so the refusal rule needs that edge named (or an `--after` whose target waits on the section the new request implements refused).
findings.text: §8 asserts "An `--after` ref names only a request that already exists, so it cannot close a cycle; a cycle can only arrive through section refs", but a section wait is satisfied by a request that is queued for that section, and that request may itself carry `--after` the older one: if request X waits on section `A#s1` and request Y is then dispatched for `A#s1` with `--after X`, X waits for `A#s1` to be declared done (which only Y's landing does) while Y waits for X to land — a cycle with no `--after`-only edge and no section-ref cycle, so a cycle check built to the stated rule accepts both, and both sit `awaiting-upstream` forever (they are not `queued`, so §14's "no request sat `queued` for more than an hour without a recorded verdict" measure does not catch it either
